agent_responses.reasoning: This design cannot proceed past the gate in its current state. The most critical blocker is the intentional logging of full card numbers and customer names without any redaction layer—this is explicitly called out in both the design doc and data flow diagram and must be resolved before any further review. Beyond that, the acceptance criteria are directionally useful but incomplete: they lack percentile definitions, measurement conditions, and duration thresholds that would make them testable. There is also no business-level success metric—catching fraud is the point of this service, yet no fraud detection KPI is defined. The absence of a rollback plan for a service sitting on the transaction critical path is a significant operational gap. Finally, no cost estimate or autoscaling ceiling is documented despite a high sustained RPS target, making budget risk unquantifiable. I recommend blocking and requiring: (1) a PII redaction design for all logs, (2) a defined log retention policy, (3) enriched acceptance criteria with percentile and test-condition specificity, (4) at least one fraud-outcome success metric, (5) a rollback procedure, and (6) a cost estimate with a compute cap before resubmission.

agent_responses.reasoning: This design cannot proceed past the design gate in its current state. The most critical issues are the intentional logging of full card PANs and customer names to CloudWatch without any redaction, and the complete absence of a PCI-DSS scope review for a service that processes card transactions. These two items alone are blocking: they represent regulatory and compliance violations that cannot be remediated post-launch cheaply. The CloudWatch log group also has no retention policy, compounding the PAN exposure. agent_responses.reasoning: This design is blocked on two independent blocking defects. First, full PAN (card numbers) and customer PII are being written to CloudWatch logs without any redaction mechanism — this is both a PCI DSS violation and a GDPR/privacy violation that cannot proceed to implementation. Second, there is no PCI DSS scope review anywhere in the design artifacts despite the service explicitly handling card transaction data. Beyond the blocking items, the log group has no retention policy (compounding the PAN-in-logs risk and creating open-ended storage cost), encryption at rest for the log group is unaddressed, and there is no cost ceiling on autoscaling for a service targeted at 5000 RPS. No cost estimate is present at this gate. All blocking concerns must be resolved — specifically: implement a PAN redaction/tokenization layer before logging, engage a QSA or internal PCI team to document scope, define log retention and encryption controls — before this design can be approved. The medium-severity cost ceiling and cost estimate gaps must also be addressed as conditions of re-submission.
